problems.prompt: A learner re-reads a worked example five times instead of trying to answer similar questions from memory. Compared to a learner who attempts and checks five times in the same span, what does the testing effect predict about their recall a week later?

choices.text: The re-reading learner will recall it better, since repetition is repetition either way
The retrieval-practice learner will recall it better, because producing an answer from memory strengthens it more than recognizing familiar material
Both will recall it equally well, since they spent the same total time studying
Neither will recall it — a week is too long for either method to matter

problems.solution: The testing effect: actively retrieving an answer from memory builds a stronger, more durable memory trace than passively re-reading the same material, even though re-reading feels easier at the time.

problems.prompt: After a concept's lesson, why does the app have you write each answer yourself instead of showing you more worked examples?

choices.text: To reduce how much content the app has to store
Because retrieving an answer from memory is what builds the memory — re-reading an example never forces that retrieval
Because worked examples are being removed from the app entirely
Because longer worked examples are harder to display on a phone screen

problems.solution: The lesson's worked example gives the first foothold on a new idea, but only an unaided retrieval — struggling a little, sometimes getting it wrong — produces the strengthening the testing effect is named for.
